1:
Who sang this and when is the first question, and the answers are far apart. John Calvin holds it clearly manifest that the psalm was composed by some other hand than David’s, and refers its complaints to that calamitous period in which the tyranny of Antiochus wasted everything; his editor adds that Geddes supposes the same persecution, that Matthias may have been the author, and that Walford agrees. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same era by another road, explaining the psalm by the situation of the saints under the Maccabees and noting what makes it singular: other national laments set the present against the former times, but none contains any like consciousness of innocence, a feature in which this psalm has no equal. Adam Clarke puts it in the captivity, and dismisses the Syriac ascription that the people and Moses sang it at Horeb: such titles, he says, are fancies to which no credit should be attached. Augustine of Hippo takes the title as the key. Korah is equivalent to the word baldness, and our Lord was crucified in the place of a skull; it is clear then that this psalm is sung to the sons of his Passion. He finds his warrant in Paul, who quoted from it by way of consolation when the Church was suffering persecution, and concludes that what we hear in it is the voice of the Martyrs.

The hearing itself draws the most comment. John Gill notes that the church in distress calls to mind past favours to encourage her faith, and that this came not only as tradition from father to son but as recorded in the writings of Moses and the prophets. C.H. Spurgeon prefers the ear to the page: among the godly the nation’s biography was preserved by oral tradition with great diligence, and to hear with the ears affects us more sensitively than to read with the eyes. He turns it on parents: schoolmasters are well enough, but godly fathers are by nature and grace the best instructors of their sons and cannot delegate the duty; when fathers are tongue-tied religiously with their offspring, need they wonder if their children’s hearts remain sin-tied? Matthew Henry observes that most psalms entitled Maschil are sorrowful ones, since afflictions give instructions, and that the many operations of providence are spoken of as a single work, many wheels making but one wheel; it is a debt, he says, which every age owes to posterity to keep an account of God’s works of wonder. Charles Ellicott reads the tradition nationally: these memories were a sacred heritage of every Hebrew, and this psalm with all the historical psalms shows how closely interwoven for the Jew were patriotism and religion.

The planting is where the readings part. John Gill takes the driven-out heathen for the Canaanites, as the Targum does, and Adam Clarke works the figure out: they were a bad tree planted in a good soil and bringing forth bad fruit with great luxuriance, which God plucked up by the roots, planting the Hebrews in its place as a good vine. Charles Ellicott says the received rendering of the last clause entirely misses the meaning and destroys the parallelism. The Hebrew word is the one used of a tree spreading its branches, and the pronoun in each clause plainly refers to Israel: thou didst afflict the peoples, but didst make them to spread. On the next verse John Gill lists the marks that the possession was the Lord’s doing and not Israel’s — the passage of Jordan as on dry land, the taking of Jericho, the smiting by the men of Ai — while Adam Clarke puts it in one line, that they conquered neither by valour nor cunning nor merit, yet were obliged to fight. Charles Ellicott notes that the light of God’s countenance stands in deliberate contrast to the hidden face later on.
4:
The turn from memory to claim is made at the word King, and it is heard in four keys. John Gill has the church claiming her interest and drawing nigh with holy boldness, asking her King for a word, since where the word of a king is, there is power. Adam Clarke makes the claim a plea from likeness: what thou wert to them, be to us; we believe in thee as they did, and though we have sinned and are in captivity we repent and turn unto thee, so command deliverances to Jacob, for we are his descendants. Charles Ellicott reads the Hebrew as an emphatic doubling — thou, even thou, art my king — and catches the psychology of the moment: what God has done in the past may be expected again, and for an instant the poet forgets the weight of his actual trouble in the faith sprung from that grateful retrospect. C.H. Spurgeon stays with the office. To whom should a people look but to their king, whose business it is to fight their battles? And he finds a reason in the name: Jacob’s long life was crowded with trials and deliverances, and his descendants are called by his name as if to typify the likeness of their experience to his, so that he who would win the blessings of Israel must share the sorrows of Jacob.

What the pushing pictures is the next question, and the English has lost it. Charles Ellicott says so outright: the image of the original is gone from our version though the Greek retained it, and it is that of a buffalo or other horned animal driving back and goring its enemies, the figure continuing in the next clause as the infuriated animal tramples its victim underfoot. Adam Clarke gives the same picture more roughly, rendering it we will toss them in the air with our horn, a metaphor taken from an ox or bull tossing into the air the dogs that attack him. John Gill keeps the horn but makes it a person: the Chaldee renders the clause through the Word, and that Word is Christ, the church’s King and the horn of salvation by which a people weak in themselves push down enemies many and mighty. C.H. Spurgeon hears no animal at all but a grapple: the fight was very close, bows were of no avail and swords failed of service, it came to daggers drawing and hand to hand wrestling, pushing and tugging — Jacob’s God renewing in the seed of Jacob their father’s wrestling.

Whether the disavowal of the bow is a vow or a memory divides the last verses. John Gill takes it as present resolve, trusting in no carnal weapon, no creature help, no arm of flesh, and gives God the whole glory of a salvation the people did not work for themselves. Adam Clarke corrects the tense: since the psalmist is speaking of what God had already done for the forefathers, the words should be read as we have not trusted. On the boasting he supplies a motive none of the others mentions. We have told the heathen how great and powerful our God is; if thou do not now deliver us by thy mighty power, they will not believe our report, but will conclude that we are held in bondage by the superior strength of their gods. John Gill keeps the boast where he keeps everything else, in Christ, who of God is made to his people wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption, so that there is always matter of glorying in him.
9:
The hinge of the psalm is the word But, and the voices differ over what it registers. Matthew Henry hears the loss of the usual tokens: thou seemest to have cast us off and our cause, and so hast put us to shame, for we boasted of the constancy of thy favour; our armies go forth as usual, but are put to flight, and we lose what we had gained. He adds the caution at once — God’s people, when they are cast down, are tempted to think themselves cast off and forsaken of God, but it is a mistake. C.H. Spurgeon insists on the cause: the patriot bard traces the change neither to the death of some human champion nor to the accidents of war, but solely to the withdrawal of Israel’s God, who seemed to have grown weary of his people and laid them aside as men lay aside leprous garments. Poverty and distress, he says, bring no shame on a people, but the Lord’s absence takes from a church everything that can ennoble it; and if the Lord be not the leader, of what avail are strong battalions? He then brings it home to his own generation, hoping none of us may have to mourn over the ministry, the Sabbath school, the missionary work and the street preaching, left to be carried on without the divine aid. Adam Clarke keeps to the history: were we to muster our tribes as our fathers did when they came out of Egypt, thou wouldst not accompany us, and the chariots of the Babylonians would soon overtake and destroy us. John Gill reads the passage of the church under the Gospel, cast off in her own eyes because afflicted and not immediately delivered, and thinks first of the ten persecutions under Rome Pagan.

How far the defeat reaches is measured differently. Charles Ellicott takes the haters spoiling for themselves to mean at their own will, an expression denoting the completeness of the overthrow: they lie absolutely at their enemies’ pleasure. Adam Clarke says the enemies, finding their strength departed, made them an easy prey. John Gill turns even the retreat inward, applying it to visible members of the church who were not valiant for the truth and deserted the cause when tribulation arose, though he notes that Arama referred it to the times of Eli. John Wesley states the outcome plainly: those not slain were carried into captivity and dispersed.

Whether the scattering dates the psalm is the sharpest question here. Adam Clarke says it most evidently alludes to the captivity, and lists the deportations under Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser and Nebuchadnezzar which left Jews in every province of the east to the present day. Charles Ellicott refuses the inference: the image of sheep appointed for the slaughter and unable to resist recalls a famous prophetic figure, but does not necessarily connect the psalm with the exile, being one likely to suggest itself in any time of helpless peril. John Gill looks past the exile to the flock of slaughter of a later age, worried not only under Rome Pagan but by the butcheries of Rome Papal.

The selling for nothing closes the section. John Gill reads it as a valuation: to sell for nought suggests that in their apprehension God had no esteem of them, as men part for nothing with what they wish to be rid of. Adam Clarke hears the slave market, except that instead of seeking profit thou hast made us a present to our enemies. Charles Ellicott works on the grammar and makes the second clause say what the first does: literally the words are for not riches, and rather than reading that God gained nothing by the sale we should render that he did not increase in the matter of their price — he set no high price on them.
13:
The reproach is felt by all four, and located in four different centuries. John Gill takes it for the common lot of Christians, which Christ and his apostles gave the saints of every age reason to expect and to esteem an honour, greater riches than the treasures of the antichristian Egypt; the byword among the heathen he reads as the names the Papists gave the reformed, calling them schismatics, heretics, fanatics, and what not. Adam Clarke keeps the Jews as the subject and finds the proverb still current: see the Hebrews, see how low the wrath of God has brought down an offending people — so that the worst curse which can be imprecated against a wicked nation is that it may become as wretched as the Jews. He then sets down the old Psalter’s rendering in its own English, where the scorning and hething come from those that are in our umgang, that is, from the neighbours all about us, and the taunt runs, when men say so befall thee, as befell him.

Charles Ellicott reads the lines as more than history. He first corrects the grammar, taking the face as a second object so that shame has covered me as to my face; then he claims that though these verses are the record of a sad reality they have also the value of a prophecy sadder still, twenty centuries of misery summed up in a few lines which have been most literally repeated — and he quotes Browning on the torture prolonged from age to age, the infamy that became Israel’s heritage, the plague of the Ghetto, the disgrace of the garb, the badge of shame and the felon’s place.

Who is doing the reproaching is the last question, and it is answered from three directions. John Gill names antichrist, to whom a mouth speaking blasphemies has been given, and who has opened it against God, blaspheming his name and his tabernacle and them that dwell in heaven. John Wesley keeps the pair of words distinct and glosses the avenger as one who executes both God’s vengeance and his own. Adam Clarke leaves the reproacher unnamed and lets the surrounding nations do the work, since it is their proverb that has made this people the standing example of what the wrath of God can do.
17:
The protest of innocence makes this psalm singular, and the roster is not equally comfortable with it. Adam Clarke flags the difficulty at once: these are bold words, but they must be understood in a qualified sense — we have not apostatised, we have not fallen into idolatry — and that much, he says, was strictly true, since the charge of idolatry could never be brought against the nation after the captivity. John Wesley makes the same reservation shorter: although we cannot excuse ourselves from many other sins, yet through thy grace we have kept ourselves from apostasy and idolatry. Matthew Henry puts the qualification into the sufferers’ own mouths — we cannot deny that we have dealt foolishly, yet we have not dealt falsely in thy covenant — and adds that though idolaters were their conquerors they entertained no more favourable thoughts of the idols; though thou hast slain us, we have continued to trust in thee. C.H. Spurgeon takes the claim at full strength. True fidelity can endure rough usage, and those who follow God for what they get will leave him when persecution is stirred up; the entire psalm might be called the martyr’s complaint, since not for sin but for righteousness did the saints suffer. Keil and Delitzsch put the same point as the logic of the passage: the church is not conscious of any apostasy, for it is suffering for the sake of its fidelity. John Gill agrees that all this came not by chance but by the counsel of God, and not for sin but for Christ’s sake and his Gospel.

Where they were broken divides the entry entirely. Charles Ellicott dissolves the dragons. The expression evidently means a wild desert place, and Aquila has an uninhabitable place; the rendering dragons arose from the resemblance of the Hebrew word to another meaning a sea monster, whereas this creature must be a wild beast, named with ostriches and with wild asses that snuff up the wind and described as uttering a mournful howl — the jackal answering those requirements best. The Greek and Latin, he adds, have in the place of affliction. Adam Clarke keeps the terror but makes it human, saying they were delivered into the hands of a fierce, cruel and murderous people, and then paints the figure anyway: like one strayed into a wilderness with no human inhabitants, hearing nothing but the hissing of serpents, the howling of beasts of prey and the terrible roaring of the lion, and expecting every moment to be devoured. John Wesley is content with a place extremely desolate, such as dragons love, and full of horror and danger. John Gill gives it a name: Rome, both Pagan and Papal, the seat of Satan the great red dragon, and the wilderness where the church is kept and fed through the times of the Papacy.

The oath that follows is put as a challenge. Adam Clarke notes that the name in question is the one by which the true God was distinguished, excluding all other objects of adoration, and explains the stretching out of hands as the ancient posture of prayer, the worshipper reaching towards the heavens or the image as if to receive the favour asked. John Gill makes the appeal an appeal indeed, God being certain to search out any such thing and punish it, and takes the whole as the church’s testimony to her steadfastness. On the last verse Keil and Delitzsch observe that Paul transfers the utterance to the New Testament church suffering in witness to the truth, or rather considers it a divine utterance coined by anticipation concerning them; Adam Clarke says the primitive Christians were in the same state, John Gill finds the accomplishment in the ten persecutions and afterwards under the Papacy, and John Wesley gives the reason in a line, that they were constant in a worship their enemies abhorred.
23:
Telling God to wake is the boldest line in the psalm, and the roster handles it carefully. John Gill begins by denying the premise: sleep does not properly fall upon God, and the Keeper of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps, his eyes always upon his people night and day. But he seems to be asleep when wicked men flourish and go on in sin with impunity, when their judgment seems to linger, and when the saints are under sore affliction and he does not appear for their deliverance — as when the disciples were in a storm and Christ was asleep, and they asked whether he cared that they perished. He awakes, in the sense prayed for here, when he stirs up himself and pleads his people’s cause thoroughly. C.H. Spurgeon gives the same denial and a franker reason for the words: God sleepeth not, but the psalmist puts it so as if on no other theory he could explain the divine inaction, since he cannot understand why the reign of tyranny and the oppression of virtue are permitted. At the thought of what the saints have endured, he joins his own voice to the great martyr cry and quotes the bard of Paradise on the slaughtered saints whose bones lie scattered on the Alpine mountains cold. Adam Clarke puts a fence round the whole manner of speaking: this is a freedom of speech which can only be allowed to inspired men, and in their mouths it is always to be figuratively understood.

The hidden face draws a rule about prayer itself. C.H. Spurgeon says we may question the Lord when his dealings are mysterious, not petulantly but piteously, being permitted to order our case with arguments and plead the right before the face of the august Majesty — though this question, he grants, is far more easily asked than answered, since it is hard in the midst of persecution to see why we are left to suffer so severely. Adam Clarke turns it into a simple request for an explanation: show us the cause why thou withdrawest from us the testimony of thy approbation.

How far down they have been brought is read two ways. John Gill offers three senses and settles on none: great declension in spiritual things and little exercise of grace; or a very low estate in temporals, their enemies setting their feet upon their necks; or even nearness to death itself. John Wesley takes it bodily and leaves it there — not only thrown down to the earth, but lying there like dead carcases.

The last plea is grounded differently by the two who touch it. John Gill rests it on the fact that God is the help of his people and a present help in time of trouble, and the only one, who can help when none else can. Adam Clarke rests it on the mercy named in the verse, asking to be ransomed from their thraldom so that they may magnify that mercy as they ought; and he notes that the Latin reads instead redeem us on account of thy name, which the old Psalter renders in its own English — help us in righteousness, and buy us, that is deliver us, that we be without dread, and all this for thy name, not for our merit.
